rv.q: Young Jean Lee's 'Straight White Men' is a wrenching, funny and ultimately devastating examination of what happens when good intentions collide with systemic inequity.
'Straight White Men,' a smart, funny and affecting play that reaffirms Lee's status as one of the most important playwrights working today.
No play, however shrewd, can change or compass the profound inequalities of American life, or even of American theater, and Lee is clever enough to know that.
Lee is not dismissive as she gently squeezes their universe into a foosball and rolls it toward an overwhelming question.
For all its clear-eyed examination of certain kinds of meanness — the most insidious of which look a lot like caring

In deconstructing the lives of these white men with all their privilege and power, Lee discovers hidden levels of deep discontent — let's bite the bullet and call it unhappiness — that indicates the kind of existential human pain common to the human condition.
Despite its imperfections, this is the sort of thoughtful, challenging and original work too rarely seen on Broadway these days.
It's a comedy about privilege that doesn't let anyone, including the audience, off the hook.
But now, by trying to lampoon whiteness, she’s made a “white” play: shallow, soporific, and all about itself.
The play isn't any good, though that won't matter, since it fulfills the first condition of success on Broadway
The overall performances, the direction, and the very smart and original writing make 'Straight White Men' a sure-fire bet and a winner for Second Stage.

At times it feels like each is waiting his turn for the next line they need to nail, but overall the cast delivers magnetic and profound performances, sandwiching harsh truths between jokes and even some adorable dance moves.
They take a funny, poignant, provocative look at family, gender roles, and 'progressive' tolerance.
It just doesn’t quite flow plausibly with these particular characters, and the energy of the play dips with its late-breaking battery of earnestness.

The play's title is still the theatrical equivalent of a reductive click-bait headline, but if viewers really watch and listen, even the queerest, brownest, and femalest audience members might find they have more in common with straight white men than they would care to admit.
This is no dysfunctional family drama; these men all care about each other. Deeply.
That may be the best message of all: Straight white guys, make room — a new group has arrived.

Understanding turns out to be in short supply.
Like so many 90-minute plays these days, 'Straight White Men' is a mildly amusing extended skit.
When a play is open to this many possible interpretations, it eventually comes to seem meaningless.
You’ll have time to think about that as the reiteration of arguments makes this 90-plus minute play feel stuck on repeat.
I can't really express how full and rich Straight White Men turned out to be for me.

It’s a bit obtuse and vague in the final moments, not giving us much of a formal conclusion of the study, but somewhere within the margin of error, deep in the statistics found, the idea of privilege and what it means to be Straight White Men is still churning and figuring itself out.
This brisk, entertaining, and deeply thought-provoking play is never strident or sentimental.
The play becomes riveting despite its contrivances and unanswered questions.
Under Shapiro's steady hand, all three actors appear totally comfortable onstage and deliver performances that go far beyond cameo status.
Under Anna D. Shapiro’s assured direction, Armie Hammer, Josh Charles, and Paul Schneider have all fully inhabited their characters; and they emerge as a family, warts and all.
This production is like a Christmas present with too much wrapping, but once you open the box, you love what’s inside.
In truth, it is often funny, sometimes exhilarating.
Armie Hammer proves especially deft with Driscoll's many maneuvers, like leaping on or off the sofa or a coffee table.
But the majority of the vignettes provide piercingly realistic moments in a woman’s life, unlike Lee’s somewhat clinical and satiric approach.
In an increasingly vitriol-fueled culture, we all might benefit from a good dose of empathy.
In fact, it would make 'Straight White Men' more of a must-see than a maybe-sit-through.
The play is stranded between genres.
Half a really funny play doesn't quite make up for the other half which is exaggerated baloney.
Lee has never been one for easy answers, but here she seems to resist even posing more pointed questions.
Still, even at 90 minutes, the play feels one-note, and bloated.
That the performances are so entertaining is the bread and butter of the show.
What we are left here with not so much as a rewarding play but an unfulfilling setup of a premise.
Straight White Men comes off as remarkably conventional, despite what seem like doth-protest-too-much attempts to market it as dark, edgy, and more challenging than it actually is.
It is also a missed opportunity play.
This critic relearned more about the role of straight white men from the Persons in Charge than from Young Jean Lee's exhausting script.
